articles.content: True Agents Model the World LAB 01 COMPUTE 02 RESEARCH 03 Docs Blog Careers 24 Book a call Start training Login Authors Prime Intellect Team Research June 5, 2026 True Agents Model the World Pretraining creates simulators , LLMs that can model their environment with high precision. RL only improves the model’s own generations. But true agents should do both at the same time: we don’t want a pure simulator, but neither do we want the LLM to only act, blind to how it will affect its environment. Instead, we want it to learn to predict its environment in response to its own actions, allowing it to more intelligently plan and respond to unexpected world dynamics. Synthetic data during pre- and midtraining achieves similar objectives, but only world modeling during RL is truly on policy. Recent

articles.content: We Asked Grok Build 0.1 to Recover a Secret Hidden in Git History Kilo Blog Subscribe Sign in We Asked Grok Build 0.1 to Recover a Secret Hidden in Git History Darko Jun 10, 2026 5 Share We wanted to test Grok Build 0.1 on a real agentic coding task from one of the world’s most popular coding benchmarks (Terminal-Bench). The background: Kilo Bench is our internal benchmark we use for new models. It’s a fork of Terminal-Bench 2.0 , integrated with the Kilo CLI . To test Grok Build 0.1, we took one of the most popular Terminal-Bench tasks called git-leak-recovery and asked Grok to execute on it. The task Imagine this: A secret got committed to a Git repository by mistake. Someone noticed and tried to make it disappear by rewinding the branch back to the commit before it. The current files hi

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: Final check: secret recovered, repo actually clean, README and unrelated commits untouched. Full checksum integrity pass. The task comes straight from Terminal-Bench, which we run on every new model through KiloBench.

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: Then the part most agents would botch: it saved the secret first, expired the reflog, re-checked, noticed the objects were still there, and ran git gc --prune=now. It verified mid-task instead of declaring victory early.

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: The secret wasn't in any visible file or commit. Grok ran git fsck --unreachable, found an orphaned commit named "feat: add scratch notes," and pulled the secret out of it.

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: A secret got committed to a Git repo, then "erased" with a branch rewind. The repo looked clean. The history looked clean. We ran Grok Build 0.1 on this exact scenario: git-leak-recovery, one of Terminal-Bench's most popular tasks. 27 steps. 41 seconds. $0.09. The human expert estimate is about 30 minutes.
